blocks.text: A 34-year-old cook arrives forty minutes after a deep-fat fryer fire. His shirt is gone, the skin of his chest is mottled with blisters, and he asks for a drink because he is so thirsty. Within hours, the burn will leak litres of plasma into the tissues, and how accurately you estimate the injured area and replace fluid will decide whether his kidneys survive.

blocks.markdown: The skin has an epidermis (barrier, keratinocytes) and a dermis (collagen, blood vessels, nerve endings, adnexal structures such as hair follicles and sweat glands from which re-epithelialisation can occur). A burn destroys these layers to varying depth. Damaged capillaries leak, inflammatory mediators cause generalised capillary permeability when the burn is large, and plasma volume falls (burn shock). Burns over about 15% of the total body surface area (TBSA) in adults, or 10% in children, generally require formal fluid resuscitation.

blocks.caption: Burn depth: clinical appearance
rows: Up to about 2 weeks, minimal scar
Blotchy red or white, slow capillary refill, may not blanch
More than 3 weeks, scarring; often needs grafting
White, waxy or leathery, may be charred
Does not re-epithelialise from the centre; needs excision and grafting

blocks.title: Total body surface area (TBSA)
blocks.text: TBSA is the percentage of the body surface with burn deeper than superficial (simple erythema is not counted). In adults, the Wallace rule of nines gives: head and neck 9%, each arm 9%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, each leg 18%, perineum 1%. The patient's own palm with the fingers is about 1% and is useful for small or scattered burns.

blocks.caption: Parkland formula using crystalloid (Hartmann's solution). Half is given in the first 8 hours from the time of injury, the rest over the next 16 hours. Variants (e.g. 2 to 3 mL/kg/%) exist, and the rate is adjusted to urine output.

blocks.title: Estimating TBSA and planning initial fluid
blocks.prompt: A man weighing 80 kg has burns to the whole of his anterior trunk and the whole of his left arm, 1 hour before arrival. Use the rule of nines and the Parkland formula to calculate the total 24-hour volume and the rate over the first 8 hours from injury.

steps.text: TBSA: anterior trunk 18% plus one arm 9%.
Half is given in the first 8 hours from injury.
He arrives 1 hour after injury, so 7 hours remain in the first 8-hour period.

blocks.answer: Total about 8.6 L in 24 hours; about 617 mL/h for the first 7 hours after arrival, then adjusted hourly to a urine output of about 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h.

blocks.markdown: **First aid and initial care.** Stop the burning process, remove clothing and jewellery, cool the burn with cool running water for 20 minutes (effective up to 3 hours after injury), keep the patient warm and cover the burn with cling film. Assess airway (singed nasal hairs, soot, hoarse voice suggest inhalation injury), give analgesia, and use fluid resuscitation guided by urine output through a catheter. Refer to a specialist burns service according to the national referral criteria (large TBSA, full thickness, face, hands, feet, genitalia, circumferential, inhalation, chemical or electrical injury, extremes of age).

**Wound healing.** Four overlapping phases: (1) *haemostasis* (platelet plug, fibrin clot); (2) *inflammation* (neutrophils then macrophages, days 1 to 4, clearing debris and bacteria); (3) *proliferation* (fibroblasts lay down collagen, angiogenesis forms granulation tissue, keratinocytes migrate, wound contracts, days 4 to about 21); (4) *remodelling* (collagen type III replaced by stronger type I over months; scar reaches about 80% of normal tensile strength). Healing by *primary intention* closes edges of a clean wound with sutures; *secondary intention* leaves a wound open to granulate and contract, used for contaminated wounds and abscess cavities.

blocks.caption: Factors that impair wound healing
rows: Infection, ischaemia, foreign body, tension, haematoma, radiation
Reduced oxygen and perfusion; prolonged inflammation
Diabetes, malnutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), anaemia, older age, obesity
Impaired collagen synthesis and immune function
Vasoconstriction and reduced tissue oxygen delivery

blocks.title: Reasoning through necrotising infection
blocks.prompt: A 58-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes has a small leg wound. She now reports severe pain far worse than the redness suggests, with fever and a heart rate of 120/min. How do you reason?

steps.text: Pain out of proportion to visible skin change suggests deep infection of fascia and muscle spreading faster than the skin can show.
Systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia) and risk factors (diabetes) increase suspicion of necrotising fasciitis.
Late signs such as crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis, and anaesthesia of the skin should not be awaited; a delayed diagnosis is the main cause of death.

Management: urgent surgical exploration and debridement, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (commonly including clindamycin to suppress toxin production), resuscitation, and repeated debridement as needed.

blocks.answer: Treat as necrotising fasciitis: do not wait for imaging or skin changes; urgent surgical debridement with antibiotics and resuscitation.

items: Pre-operative: treat existing infection, optimise glucose, stop smoking where possible; clip rather than shave hair, if removal is necessary.
Skin preparation with an alcoholic antiseptic such as chlorhexidine in alcohol.
Intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis given within 60 minutes before incision when indicated, not prolonged postoperatively for routine clean surgery.
Intra-operative: asepsis, minimise operative time, maintain normothermia and oxygenation, careful tissue handling.
Post-operative: wound surveillance, hand hygiene, and early recognition of infection.

blocks.title: Classifying wounds for infection risk
blocks.text: Clean wounds (no viscus opened) have about 1 to 2% infection risk; clean-contaminated (viscus opened under control) higher; contaminated (spillage, acute inflammation) and dirty (pus, perforation) the highest. Antibiotic prophylaxis is most clearly beneficial in clean-contaminated procedures and for implants.

points: Burn depth is judged by appearance, capillary refill and sensation; TBSA by the rule of nines or the patient's palm.
Initial burn care: cooling, cling film, airway assessment, analgesia and Parkland-based fluids adjusted to urine output.
Healing proceeds through haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling and is impaired by ischaemia, infection, diabetes, malnutrition, steroids and smoking.
SSI prevention uses timely prophylactic antibiotics, skin antisepsis and good technique; pain out of proportion with toxicity demands urgent evaluation for necrotising infection.

questions.stem: A scald produces a pink, moist wound with intact blisters that blanches briskly and is very painful. What is the depth?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: blisters, pink, moist, brisk blanching and marked pain.
distractorRationale.b: Full thickness is painless and leathery.
distractorRationale.c: Epidermal burns are dry without blisters.
distractorRationale.d: Deep partial burns are blotchy, with slow capillary refill and reduced sensation.

questions.explanation: Superficial partial-thickness burns involve the upper dermis, leaving rich blood supply and nerve endings, so they blister, blanch and hurt. They usually heal in about two weeks.

questions.stem: A patient has a dry, white, leathery area of burn with no pain on pinprick. What does this indicate?

options.text: Full-thickness burn likely needing excision and grafting
Superficial burn that will heal without a scar
A burn that can be managed with a simple dressing alone

questions.correctOptionText: Full-thickness burn likely needing excision and grafting

distractorRationale.a: Correct: dermal nerve endings and appendages are destroyed.
distractorRationale.b: Superficial burns are red and painful.
distractorRationale.c: Appearance reflects depth, not first aid quality.
distractorRationale.d: A full-thickness burn will not heal adequately with dressings alone, except tiny areas.

questions.explanation: Full-thickness burns destroy the entire dermis including nerve endings, hence they are insensate and leathery. They cannot regenerate epithelium from within and usually require excision and skin grafting.

questions.stem: A smoker with poorly controlled diabetes has a laparotomy wound that is slow to heal. Which mechanism best explains impaired healing?

options.text: Reduced tissue oxygen delivery and impaired inflammatory and fibroblast function

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced tissue oxygen delivery and impaired inflammatory and fibroblast function

distractorRationale.a: Correct: vasoconstriction from smoking and hyperglycaemia impair perfusion and cell function.
distractorRationale.b: Excess collagen causes hypertrophic scars, not delayed healing.
distractorRationale.d: Neutrophil function is impaired by hyperglycaemia.

questions.explanation: Smoking causes vasoconstriction and carboxyhaemoglobin formation, reducing tissue oxygen, and hyperglycaemia impairs leucocyte and fibroblast function. Together they delay all phases of healing and increase infection risk.

questions.stem: Which measure best reduces the risk of surgical site infection in an elective colorectal operation?

options.text: Intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision
Shaving the abdomen with a razor the night before
Giving antibiotics for 7 days after surgery routinely
Applying antibiotic ointment to the skin after closure alone

questions.correctOptionText: Intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision

distractorRationale.a: Correct: timing ensures tissue levels at the moment of incision.
distractorRationale.b: Razor shaving causes microabrasions and increases infection; clipping is preferred.
distractorRationale.c: Routine prolonged postoperative antibiotics do not add benefit and promote resistance.
distractorRationale.d: Topical ointment alone is not an evidence-based prevention strategy.

questions.explanation: Prophylactic antibiotics are effective only when tissue concentrations are adequate at incision, so they are given shortly before the knife touches the skin. Razor shaving and prolonged courses are not beneficial and may harm.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has a minor groin abscess drained yesterday. He now has fever 39.1 degrees C, heart rate 124/min, and severe pain extending beyond the erythema, with dusky skin and a few bullae. What is the priority?

options.text: Urgent surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation
Oral flucloxacillin and review in 48 hours

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: necrotising infection needs source control without delay.
distractorRationale.b: Oral antibiotics are inadequate and delay surgery.
distractorRationale.c: Imaging must not delay surgical exploration.
distractorRationale.d: Observation allows rapid spread and death.

questions.explanation: Pain beyond the visible margin, systemic toxicity and dusky bullous skin indicate necrotising soft-tissue infection. Mortality rises with each hour of delay, so urgent debridement, antibiotics and resuscitation are required.

questions.stem: Routine prophylactic antibiotics should be continued for 5 to 7 days after uncomplicated clean surgery to prevent surgical site infection.
questions.explanation: Evidence supports a single pre-incision dose, sometimes repeated for long operations or large blood loss. Prolonged courses do not lower infection rates and increase resistance and adverse effects.

questions.stem: A 60 kg woman has 40% TBSA burns. Using the Parkland formula of 4 mL/kg/% TBSA, calculate the volume of crystalloid, in mL, to be given in the first 8 hours from injury (half of the 24-hour total).
questions.explanation: The 24-hour total is 4 x 60 x 40 = 9600 mL, and half of it, 4800 mL, is given in the first 8 hours after injury. The infusion is then titrated to urine output rather than followed blindly.

questions.stem: A 70 kg man with 30% TBSA burns reaches hospital 2 hours after injury. Using the Parkland formula (4 mL/kg/% TBSA, half in the first 8 hours from injury), calculate the initial infusion rate in mL/h needed to deliver that first half over the remaining time.
questions.explanation: The total is 4 x 70 x 30 = 8400 mL, so half is 4200 mL. Two of the first 8 hours have elapsed, so 4200 mL must be given over 6 hours, which is 700 mL/h.

questions.stem: A diabetic smoker has a dehisced abdominal wound with slough. Describe the phases of normal wound healing and explain how these factors impair them.
markingGuide: Inflammation: neutrophils then macrophages clear debris and bacteria
Proliferation: fibroblasts, collagen, angiogenesis, epithelialisation, contraction
Remodelling: type III to type I collagen, increased tensile strength over months
Diabetes: impaired leucocyte and fibroblast function, microvascular disease, infection risk
Other factors such as malnutrition, steroids, infection, ischaemia
questions.explanation: Healing is an overlapping sequence of haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling, each needing oxygen, nutrients and intact cellular function. Smoking and diabetes degrade perfusion and cell function, delaying every phase.

questions.stem: Describe how you would recognise necrotising soft-tissue infection and the principles of treatment, contrasting this with a simple wound infection.
markingGuide: Simple wound infection: local erythema, warmth, purulent discharge, minimal systemic upset, treated with drainage and antibiotics
Necrotising infection: pain out of proportion, rapid spread, systemic toxicity, shock
Late signs: bullae, dusky skin, crepitus, anaesthesia
Risk factors: diabetes, immunosuppression, injecting drug use, recent surgery
Clinical diagnosis; do not delay for imaging
Urgent surgical exploration and debridement, repeated as necessary
Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, often with clindamycin for toxin suppression
questions.explanation: Necrotising infection spreads along fascial planes faster than skin signs develop, so recognition relies on pain, toxicity and risk factors. Surgical debridement plus antibiotics and resuscitation is essential and cannot wait for confirmation.
